newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Inside Canberra-Unfair dismissal laws still unfair.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Inside Canberra-Unfair dismissal laws still unfair.

text.p: The provision in the last month's small business package to exempt new employees from access to unfair dismissals entitlements for their first 12 months was in itself an admission that the new unfair dismissals legislation was not what most employers thought they were going to get from the Howard Government.
This point was confirmed in the Senate (March 26) by no less an authority than the Leader of the Government in the Senate, Senator Robert Hill.
He was replying to Greens Senator Dee Margetts who expressed concern about the security of new employees if they could be dismissed with relative impunity.
Senator Hill said the government believed the unfair dismissals law was a disincentive for employers to take on more labor.
He added: "Although they have been improved, they are still a disincentive to small business."
Incidentally a study by consultancy Arthur Robinson and Hedderwicks of the new legislation again demonstrates how careful employers have to be.

For example, if an employee is guilty of serious misconduct, such as theft from the workplace or assaulting a client, an employer may dismiss the guilty employee summarily -- that is, without notice or pay in lieu of notice.
But first the employer must give the employee an opportunity of explaining his or her conduct.
But Arthur Robinson and Hedderwicks advises that it might still be wise to give pay in lieu of notice even for serious misconduct.
"Where pay in lieu of notice has been given, the dismissed employee bears the evidentiary burden of proving that the dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable."
"In cases of summary dismissal the employer has to prove that summary dismissal was justified in the circumstances of that particular case."
